script.opening: (Mother, exhausted, anxious; Anaya wriggling on her lap.) "Anaya's eczema is really bad again — she's scratching all night, none of us are sleeping. The doctor gave us a steroid cream but … I looked it up and I'm scared of steroids. Won't they thin her skin, or get into her body? I've just been using moisturiser, but it's not enough. What should I do?"

facts.text: "It's all red and sore. It's been bad for a while now and it just keeps getting worse" — 3 weeks. Inside elbows, behind knees, cheeks and neck. Will show the skin on camera: red, dry, scratched patches; no weeping or yellow crusts.
"She wakes up scratching most of the night. In the day she's grumpy and scratching."
"Not that I've noticed. She's not been poorly, just itchy." No weeping, crusting, blisters or punched-out sores; no fever.

"I use it, but it's not enough. I'd have to check what we wash her with" — emollient twice a day, a small tub lasting a month; bubble bath and baby wash in the bath. Hydrocortisone 1% cream prescribed 2 months ago — unopened.
Eczema since 4 months old. No food reactions known. Wool jumpers make it worse. Dad has asthma. Anaya is otherwise healthy, growing well, immunisations up to date. No medicines, no allergies.
Lives with Mum (Priya, pharmacy dispenser on maternity leave from a second baby due in 3 months) and Dad. Everyone exhausted.
"That they thin the skin and get into the body. She's so small. I don't want to be the one who damages her skin." Read online about "steroid withdrawal".

Worried, protective, wants a non-steroid option: "Something safe that isn't a steroid, I suppose. I just want her to sleep." If the doctor dismisses the fear ("just use it"), she nods but won't use it. If the fear is acknowledged and answered with how much, where and for how long, she relaxes: "So it's not like using it forever?" and "I think I can use the cream now that I understand it."

ice.ideas: "Steroids will thin her skin or get into her body — moisturiser is safer."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — fear of harming her child with a medicine she has read frightening things about; everyone exhausted from no sleep.
ice.expectations: "Something safe that isn't a steroid — so she can sleep."

cues: "I looked it up." — ask what she read.
"None of us are sleeping." — impact on the family.
"I don't want to be the one who damages her skin." — the fear to answer.

checkpoints.text: Assesses the flare and its IMPACT (extent, itch, SLEEP disturbance) and checks for INFECTION (bacterial weeping/crusting; eczema herpeticum — urgent), and what treatment is actually being used

VALIDATES the steroid fear as understandable then CORRECTS it accurately — correctly-used topical steroids are safe; thinning relates to prolonged potent misuse, not appropriate short courses; and under-treatment from fear is itself harmful
Establishes EMOLLIENTS as the cornerstone — generous, frequent, soap substitute, continued when clear, prescribed in large quantities (250–500 g a week for a child) — and demonstrates use

Explains correct TOPICAL STEROID use: potency matched to site/severity (NICE CG57: mild for face and neck; moderate/potent for only 7–14 days in axillae/groin), short bursts to control flares then step down, applied to active eczema only, with the FINGERTIP-UNIT amount guide
Addresses TRIGGERS and scratch management, recognises/treats INFECTION (bacterial; eczema herpeticum urgent), and knows when to escalate/refer to dermatology, with a written step-up/step-down plan
RESPECTS and ANSWERS the fear rather than overriding it — building trust and the adherence that determines eczema control — and acknowledges the family’s sleeplessness/distress
Makes the mother a confident treater by checking understanding and giving a clear, believable regimen
Safety-nets and follows up: infection red flags (urgent for eczema herpeticum), what to do for flares, emollient/steroid plan, and review — trust-building, evidence-based eczema care

worked.txt: "Nobody sleeping and Anaya scratching all night — that’s really tough, and we can do much better than this. Can you show me her skin on the camera, and send a couple of photos? If anything looks infected, I’ll see her in person today. Then let’s sort out a plan you feel comfortable with."
"Your worry about steroids is completely understandable — there’s a lot of frightening stuff online, and you’re trying to protect her. Let me give you the actual facts so you can decide confidently."

"Used properly — the right strength, in short bursts to settle a flare — steroid creams are safe and effective. The skin-thinning worry comes from strong steroids used for a long time in the wrong places, not from this. And honestly, leaving the eczema raw is the thing that harms her — the itch, the sleep loss, the infection risk."

"The foundation is moisturiser — lots of it, several times a day, and as her soap. Keep it up even when she’s clear. I’ll prescribe big tubs — a toddler can easily get through 250 to 500 grams a week. Good moisturising means fewer flares and less steroid."

"For the flare, use the steroid once a day on the red, sore bits only, until it settles, then stop. Put the moisturiser on first and leave a gap of about 20 to 30 minutes before the steroid. Here’s how much — a ‘fingertip’ covers an area the size of two adult hands. It’s controlled and short — not forever."

"If the skin weeps, crusts golden, or you see clusters of little blisters and she’s unwell — that last one needs same-day help. Let’s avoid soaps and triggers, and I’ll write the plan down. Come back if it’s not settling and we’ll step things up."

f.learning: An atopic eczema flare with topical-steroid phobia is, above all, an adherence and trust problem. Assess the flare and its impact — extent, itch and especially sleep disturbance (a key severity/family-impact marker) — and check for infection (bacterial weeping/golden crusting; eczema herpeticum, with clustered punched-out vesicles, rapid worsening or an unwell child, which is urgent). Steroid phobia is extremely common and drives under-treatment, so do not dismiss it: validate it as understandable given conflicting online information, then correct it with accurate facts — topical steroids used correctly (potency matched to site and severity, short bursts to control flares) are safe and effective; skin thinning is associated with prolonged use of potent steroids on inappropriate sites rather than appropriate short courses; and under-treating eczema from steroid fear prolongs the child’s itch, sleeplessness, infection risk and suffering, so the fear itself causes harm. Establish emollients as the cornerstone (generous, frequent, used as a soap substitute, continued even when clear, prescribed in large quantities — children commonly need 250–500 g a week, NICE CG57) and explain correct steroid use (NICE CG57 potency by site: mild for face and neck, moderate or potent for only 7–14 days in axillae and groin; once or twice daily, NICE TA81) with the fingertip-unit guide (one FTU covers two adult hands, BAD 2024), applied to active eczema only, then stepped down. Address triggers and scratch management, recognise and treat infection (bacterial: NICE NG190, antibiotics only if needed; eczema herpeticum needs immediate systemic aciclovir and same-day referral, with face-to-face assessment of any suspected infection), and know when to escalate to dermatology, providing a written step-up/step-down plan. The hidden agenda is a protective fear born of wanting to keep the child safe, with distress at the family’s sleeplessness and helplessness beneath; respect and answer the fear rather than overriding it, build trust, and give a clear regimen she believes in — turning her into a confident treater, because adherence is the whole game in eczema.

knowledge.guideline: NICE CG57 (2007, updated 2023) · NICE TA81 · NICE NG190 · MHRA Drug Safety Update (September 2021; May 2024) · BAD topical corticosteroids leaflet (2024)
knowledge.summary: Emollients are the base of care, and a topical steroid of the right strength used for short bursts treats flares safely. Under-treatment through fear of steroids is the common harm.

points.t: NICE CG57: leave-on emollients for all children with atopic eczema, used even when the skin is clear and as a soap substitute; children commonly need 250–500 g a week. Do not offer emollient bath additives (2023 update).

NICE CG57: mild potency for the face and neck (moderate for 3–5 days only in severe facial flares); moderate or potent for 7–14 days only in vulnerable sites such as the axillae and groin; no very potent steroid in children without specialist advice; no potent steroid under 12 months without specialist advice. Apply once or twice daily only (NICE TA81).

One fingertip unit (from the tip of an adult index finger to the first crease) covers an area the size of two adult hands (BAD leaflet, 2024). Apply to active eczema only, until the flare settles, then stop.

points.h: Safety facts for the steroid-phobic parent
points.t: NICE CG57: the benefits of topical steroids outweigh the risks when they are used correctly. MHRA (September 2021) links topical steroid withdrawal reactions to long-term, frequent or inappropriate use, mainly of moderate to high potency products. Packs are being relabelled with their potency (MHRA, May 2024).

NICE CG57: do not use antihistamines routinely. A 7–14-day trial of a sedating antihistamine can be offered to children aged 6 months and over during a flare with significant sleep disturbance; dose per BNFC.

Eczema herpeticum (clustered punched-out erosions or vesicles, rapid worsening, unwell): immediate systemic aciclovir and same-day referral (NICE CG57). Bacterial infection: NICE NG190 — no routine antibiotic if not systemically unwell; oral flucloxacillin when needed, dose per BNFC. Urgent referral for severe eczema not responding to optimal topical treatment after 1 week (NICE CG57).

dg.d: Open question; let the mother describe the flare, the sleepless nights and her fear of steroids in her own words.
Explored the whole family’s sleep loss, daytime impact on Anaya, and the mother’s online research.
Video inspection of affected skin with a low threshold for face-to-face review; checked the potency on record; asked about emollient quantity and soaps.
Flare of atopic eczema vs secondary bacterial infection vs eczema herpeticum; irritant triggers; possible under-treatment.
Screened for eczema herpeticum and systemic illness; knew immediate aciclovir and same-day referral are needed.
Named an under-treated flare of atopic eczema and explained it in plain language.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Emollients 250–500 g a week, soap substitute; mild or moderate steroid by site, once or twice daily, short burst, fingertip units; written plan.
Sleep and itch (nails, clothing, sedating antihistamine option), irritants, parental exhaustion.
Review in a week; same-day advice for blisters or unwell; step up or refer if not settling.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “I’m scared of steroids” and “none of us are sleeping” and explored both.
Idea (steroids thin the skin and enter the body), concern (harming her child), expectation (a safe non-steroid option, sleep).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — fear of harming her child with a medicine she has read frightening things about; everyone exhausted from no sleep — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello, Mrs Sandhu, I’m Dr Evans. I can see Anaya’s eczema has been giving you all a hard time. Tell me what’s been happening.
model.why: Open question that acknowledges the family’s distress

model.text: It’s really bad again. She’s scratching all night and none of us are sleeping. The doctor gave us a steroid cream, but I looked it up and I’m scared of steroids. Won’t they thin her skin or get into her body? I’ve just been using moisturiser, but it’s not enough.

Thank you for being so honest about that. Your worry is really important, and I want to answer it properly. Can I first ask a few questions and have a look at her skin on camera, then we’ll talk about the cream and make a plan you’re comfortable with?
model.why: Validates the fear early and sets the agenda

model.text: Yes, okay.
Where on her body is it worst, and how long has this flare been going on?
model.why: Establishes extent and duration of the flare

model.text: It’s all red and sore. It’s been bad for a while now and it just keeps getting worse.
You said nobody is sleeping. How many times is she waking, and is the itch stopping her playing or eating during the day?
model.why: Uses sleep and daytime impact as markers of severity

model.text: She wakes up scratching most of the night. In the day she’s grumpy and scratching.
Two important checks. Is any of the skin weeping, crusted or yellow? And have you seen clusters of little blisters or punched-out sores, or has she been feverish or unwell in herself?
model.why: Screens for bacterial infection and eczema herpeticum

model.text: Not that I’ve noticed. She’s not been poorly, just itchy.
That’s reassuring. Could you show me her skin on the camera, including any areas that look different?
model.why: Examines what is possible on video; would convert to face to face if unclear

model.text: (Shows the affected skin.) This is what it looks like.
Thank you. How much moisturiser are you getting through, how often do you put it on, and what do you wash her with?
model.why: Checks actual treatment use and irritants

model.text: I use it, but it’s not enough. I’d have to check what we wash her with.
Tell me a bit more about what you read about steroids. What worries you most?
model.why: Explores the specific fear rather than assuming it

model.text: That they thin the skin and get into the body. She’s so small. I don’t want to be the one who damages her skin.
That’s a loving reason to be careful, and a lot of what’s online is frightening and confusing. What were you hoping we could do today?
model.why: Validates the protective motive and elicits expectations

model.text: Something safe that isn’t a steroid, I suppose. I just want her to sleep.

Can I share the facts, and then you decide? The skin-thinning problems come from strong steroids used for long periods in the wrong places. The cream for a flare in a child is a milder strength, used once or twice a day on the red patches only, for a short burst until it settles, then stopped. Used like that, the benefits clearly outweigh the risks.
model.why: Corrects the misconception with accurate potency and duration facts

model.text: So it’s not like using it forever?

Exactly. And there’s another side: leaving the eczema untreated isn’t risk-free either. The itch, the lost sleep and the broken skin, which lets infection in, are harms too. I’ll check your record to confirm the strength of the cream you were given, so we’re sure it’s the right one for where you’ll use it.
model.why: Explains the harm of under-treatment and checks potency against site

model.text: I hadn’t thought of it like that.

Here’s how much to use: squeeze a line from the tip of your finger to the first crease. That amount covers an area the size of two of your hands. Most flares settle within a week or two, and then you stop.
model.why: Teaches the fingertip unit and a clear stop point

model.text: The moisturiser is the most important part and you can use lots: several times a day, as her soap too, and carry on when her skin is clear. I’ll prescribe big tubs so you don’t run out. Put it on first, wait about half an hour, then the steroid on the red areas.
model.why: Emollients as the cornerstone, prescribed in quantity, with application order

model.text: I can do that. What about the nights?

Keep her nails short, cotton clothes, and swap the bubble bath for the moisturiser. If sleep is still very bad during this flare, a short course of a sleepy antihistamine for a week or two is an option. Would you like me to write all of this down as a plan?
model.why: Addresses sleep and triggers, offers a written plan

model.text: Yes please. I think I can use the cream now that I understand it.

If the skin starts weeping or crusting yellow, call us. If you see clusters of blisters or sores that look punched out, or she becomes feverish or unwell, that needs to be seen the same day, because it can be a herpes infection that needs treatment straight away.
model.why: Specific infection safety-net including eczema herpeticum

model.text: Okay, blisters or unwell means same day.
Just so I know I’ve explained it well, how will you use the two creams tonight?
Lots of moisturiser, then half an hour later a fingertip of the steroid on the red bits, once or twice a day, and stop when it settles.
That’s exactly right. I’ll see you both in a week, or sooner if it isn’t improving, and if it hasn’t settled with all this we can step up or ask a skin specialist.

social.t: Broken sleep affects the whole household. Ask how the parents are coping; a named plan reduces helplessness.
NICE CG57 advises a supply of emollient at nursery or school so it can be applied during the day.

legal.t: The parent consents on Anaya’s behalf; share information clearly so the decision is truly informed (GMC Decision making and consent, 2020).

professional.t: MHRA (September 2021): tell patients to use topical steroids at the right potency and for the right duration; withdrawal reactions relate to long-term inappropriate use. Check the potency issued matches the site.
NICE CG57: give verbal and written information with a demonstration of how to apply treatments.

community.t: National Eczema Society for parent information; the community pharmacist can reinforce technique and quantities.
The health visitor can support with sleep and treatment routines for under-5s.

redFlags: Clustered punched-out erosions or vesicles, rapid worsening, fever or an unwell child — possible eczema herpeticum, same-day
Weeping, crusting or spreading infection with systemic upset
Severe eczema not responding after 1 week of optimal topical treatment — urgent referral
Faltering growth or concerns about care
psychosocial: Sleep loss for the child and parents
Where the steroid fear came from and how strongly it is held
Nursery, routines and who applies the treatment
ice: Idea: “Steroids will thin her skin or get into her body”
Concern: being the one who harms her child; nobody sleeping
Expectation: a safe option that isn’t a steroid

playbook.diagnosis: “This is a flare of atopic eczema that isn’t being fully treated. I don’t see signs of infection from what you’ve told me, and we’ll keep watching for them.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Think of her skin as a leaky wall. The moisturiser patches the wall every day. The steroid is the fire extinguisher for a flare — a short, controlled burst, then you put it away.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve held back the steroid because you want to protect her. Using it the right way, for a short time, is also protecting her — from the itch and the sleepless nights.”
management.psychosocial: Plan around bedtime: nails, cotton clothing, emollient routine, and a short sedating antihistamine course if sleep stays very poor during the flare.
sharedPlan: Emollient generously several times a day and as soap substitute; large tubs prescribed
Topical steroid of the right potency for the site, once or twice daily, fingertip units, until settled then stop
safetyNet: Blisters, punched-out sores, fever or unwell — same-day review
Weeping or crusting — contact the practice; review in a week, refer if not settling

pitfalls.intro: This station is about trust. Candidates fail when they either brush the fear aside or give in to it, and when they forget to check for infection.

items.fail: Telling her steroids are “completely safe” before asking what she read.
items.why: The fear is the hidden agenda. Dismissing it leads to a parent who agrees in the room and doesn’t use the cream at home.
items.fix: Ask “What worries you most?” then answer that specific worry with accurate facts.

items.fail: Giving more moisturiser only, because the mother prefers it.
items.why: NICE CG57 uses stepped care; a flare needs a topical steroid. Under-treatment prolongs itch and sleep loss.
items.fix: Explain that emollient is the base and the steroid is a short burst for flares.

items.fail: No check for eczema herpeticum or bacterial infection.
items.why: Missing eczema herpeticum is a safety failure; it needs immediate aciclovir and same-day referral.
items.fix: Ask about blisters, punched-out sores, weeping, crusting and fever in every flare.

items.why: Vague advice leads to under-dosing and stop-start use.
items.fix: Fingertip units, once or twice daily, to red areas only, until settled, and plenty of emollient.

items.fail: No written plan and no check that she understood.
items.why: NICE CG57 advises verbal and written information with demonstration.
items.fix: Offer a written plan and use teach-back: “How will you use the creams tonight?”

items.why: Sleep loss is what brought her in. Leaving it out misses her real agenda.
items.fix: Address night-time itch directly and mention the short sedating antihistamine option.

Eczema herpeticum same day; bacterial signs; teach-back; review in a week.

avoid.instead: "Used at the right strength for short bursts, the benefits clearly outweigh the risks. Let me explain where the thinning worry comes from."
avoid.why: Blanket reassurance sounds dismissive and is not accurate; honest facts build trust.

SCA_MODELS.text: The moisturiser is the most important part and you can use lots: several times a day, as her soap too, and carry on when her skin is clear. I’ll prescribe big tubs so you don’t run out. Put it on first, wait about half an hour, then the steroid on the red areas.
SCA_MODELS.why: Emollients as the cornerstone, prescribed in quantity, with application order

SCA_MODELS.text: I can do that. What about the nights?

Keep her nails short, cotton clothes, and swap the bubble bath for the moisturiser. If sleep is still very bad during this flare, a short course of a sleepy antihistamine for a week or two is an option. Would you like me to write all of this down as a plan?
SCA_MODELS.why: Addresses sleep and triggers, offers a written plan

SCA_MODELS.text: Yes please. I think I can use the cream now that I understand it.

If the skin starts weeping or crusting yellow, call us. If you see clusters of blisters or sores that look punched out, or she becomes feverish or unwell, that needs to be seen the same day, because it can be a herpes infection that needs treatment straight away.
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific infection safety-net including eczema herpeticum

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay, blisters or unwell means same day.
Just so I know I’ve explained it well, how will you use the two creams tonight?
Lots of moisturiser, then half an hour later a fingertip of the steroid on the red bits, once or twice a day, and stop when it settles.
That’s exactly right. I’ll see you both in a week, or sooner if it isn’t improving, and if it hasn’t settled with all this we can step up or ask a skin specialist.

SCA_STEM.name: Anaya Sandhu
SCA_STEM.recent: Eczema flare. Topical steroid issued at a previous consultation; mother reports she has not been using it.
SCA_STEM.reason: Video consultation: eczema worse, scratching at night, family not sleeping.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE CG57 (2007, updated 2023) · NICE TA81 · NICE NG190 · MHRA Drug Safety Update (September 2021; May 2024) · BAD topical corticosteroids leaflet (2024)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Emollients are the base of care, and a topical steroid of the right strength used for short bursts treats flares safely. Under-treatment through fear of steroids is the common harm.

points.t: NICE CG57: leave-on emollients for all children with atopic eczema, used even when the skin is clear and as a soap substitute; children commonly need 250–500 g a week. Do not offer emollient bath additives (2023 update).

NICE CG57: mild potency for the face and neck (moderate for 3–5 days only in severe facial flares); moderate or potent for 7–14 days only in vulnerable sites such as the axillae and groin; no very potent steroid in children without specialist advice; no potent steroid under 12 months without specialist advice. Apply once or twice daily only (NICE TA81).

One fingertip unit (from the tip of an adult index finger to the first crease) covers an area the size of two adult hands (BAD leaflet, 2024). Apply to active eczema only, until the flare settles, then stop.

points.h: Safety facts for the steroid-phobic parent
points.t: NICE CG57: the benefits of topical steroids outweigh the risks when they are used correctly. MHRA (September 2021) links topical steroid withdrawal reactions to long-term, frequent or inappropriate use, mainly of moderate to high potency products. Packs are being relabelled with their potency (MHRA, May 2024).

NICE CG57: do not use antihistamines routinely. A 7–14-day trial of a sedating antihistamine can be offered to children aged 6 months and over during a flare with significant sleep disturbance; dose per BNFC.

Eczema herpeticum (clustered punched-out erosions or vesicles, rapid worsening, unwell): immediate systemic aciclovir and same-day referral (NICE CG57). Bacterial infection: NICE NG190 — no routine antibiotic if not systemically unwell; oral flucloxacillin when needed, dose per BNFC. Urgent referral for severe eczema not responding to optimal topical treatment after 1 week (NICE CG57).

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; let the mother describe the flare, the sleepless nights and her fear of steroids in her own words.
Explored the whole family’s sleep loss, daytime impact on Anaya, and the mother’s online research.
Picked up “I’m scared of steroids” and “none of us are sleeping” and explored both.
Idea (steroids thin the skin and enter the body), concern (harming her child), expectation (a safe non-steroid option, sleep).
Video inspection of affected skin with a low threshold for face-to-face review; checked the potency on record; asked about emollient quantity and soaps.
Flare of atopic eczema vs secondary bacterial infection vs eczema herpeticum; irritant triggers; possible under-treatment.
Screened for eczema herpeticum and systemic illness; knew immediate aciclovir and same-day referral are needed.
Named an under-treated flare of atopic eczema and explained it in plain language.
Emollients 250–500 g a week, soap substitute; mild or moderate steroid by site, once or twice daily, short burst, fingertip units; written plan.
Sleep and itch (nails, clothing, sedating antihistamine option), irritants, parental exhaustion.
Review in a week; same-day advice for blisters or unwell; step up or refer if not settling.

social.t: Broken sleep affects the whole household. Ask how the parents are coping; a named plan reduces helplessness.
NICE CG57 advises a supply of emollient at nursery or school so it can be applied during the day.

legal.t: The parent consents on Anaya’s behalf; share information clearly so the decision is truly informed (GMC Decision making and consent, 2020).

professional.t: MHRA (September 2021): tell patients to use topical steroids at the right potency and for the right duration; withdrawal reactions relate to long-term inappropriate use. Check the potency issued matches the site.
NICE CG57: give verbal and written information with a demonstration of how to apply treatments.

community.t: National Eczema Society for parent information; the community pharmacist can reinforce technique and quantities.
The health visitor can support with sleep and treatment routines for under-5s.

redFlags: Clustered punched-out erosions or vesicles, rapid worsening, fever or an unwell child — possible eczema herpeticum, same-day
Weeping, crusting or spreading infection with systemic upset
Severe eczema not responding after 1 week of optimal topical treatment — urgent referral
Faltering growth or concerns about care
psychosocial: Sleep loss for the child and parents
Where the steroid fear came from and how strongly it is held
Nursery, routines and who applies the treatment
ice: Idea: “Steroids will thin her skin or get into her body”
Concern: being the one who harms her child; nobody sleeping
Expectation: a safe option that isn’t a steroid

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “This is a flare of atopic eczema that isn’t being fully treated. I don’t see signs of infection from what you’ve told me, and we’ll keep watching for them.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Think of her skin as a leaky wall. The moisturiser patches the wall every day. The steroid is the fire extinguisher for a flare — a short, controlled burst, then you put it away.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve held back the steroid because you want to protect her. Using it the right way, for a short time, is also protecting her — from the itch and the sleepless nights.”
management.psychosocial: Plan around bedtime: nails, cotton clothing, emollient routine, and a short sedating antihistamine course if sleep stays very poor during the flare.
sharedPlan: Emollient generously several times a day and as soap substitute; large tubs prescribed
Topical steroid of the right potency for the site, once or twice daily, fingertip units, until settled then stop
safetyNet: Blisters, punched-out sores, fever or unwell — same-day review
Weeping or crusting — contact the practice; review in a week, refer if not settling

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is about trust. Candidates fail when they either brush the fear aside or give in to it, and when they forget to check for infection.

items.fail: Telling her steroids are “completely safe” before asking what she read.
items.why: The fear is the hidden agenda. Dismissing it leads to a parent who agrees in the room and doesn’t use the cream at home.
items.fix: Ask “What worries you most?” then answer that specific worry with accurate facts.

items.fail: Giving more moisturiser only, because the mother prefers it.
items.why: NICE CG57 uses stepped care; a flare needs a topical steroid. Under-treatment prolongs itch and sleep loss.
items.fix: Explain that emollient is the base and the steroid is a short burst for flares.

items.fail: No check for eczema herpeticum or bacterial infection.
items.why: Missing eczema herpeticum is a safety failure; it needs immediate aciclovir and same-day referral.
items.fix: Ask about blisters, punched-out sores, weeping, crusting and fever in every flare.

items.why: Vague advice leads to under-dosing and stop-start use.
items.fix: Fingertip units, once or twice daily, to red areas only, until settled, and plenty of emollient.

items.fail: No written plan and no check that she understood.
items.why: NICE CG57 advises verbal and written information with demonstration.
items.fix: Offer a written plan and use teach-back: “How will you use the creams tonight?”

items.why: Sleep loss is what brought her in. Leaving it out misses her real agenda.
items.fix: Address night-time itch directly and mention the short sedating antihistamine option.
